_source.read: 2026-10-12, read-only, from branch origin/master (production, c0515922, last commit 4 Oct 2026) via git show origin/master:public/changelog.html and git show origin/master:public/changelog-archive.json. Local branch main is stale (last commit 9 Sep, 2,636 commits) and was not used; the September read (2026-09-16) used main when it still matched production.
_source.parse_rule:
One public release = one
block. version = .timeline-version, date = .tl__date, title = the

link text, kind = the .tag chip. A bullet = one

……

paragraph inside .tl__body; bullet_leads carries each bullet's bolded lead sentence.
_source.verification_of_337: The changelog prose claims "337 releases before 1.0" in three places (lines 328, 590, 604) and a figure block (line 608). Independently confirmed by counting the archive: changelog-archive.json .entries has exactly 337 items. The write-up's 337 REPRODUCES. Re-checked 2026-10-12 on origin/master: changelog-archive.json .entries still has 337 items.
_source.reparse_check_2026_10_12: The ten September entries were re-parsed with the same rule and match field for field (version, date, kind, title, every bullet lead); the only difference is that the new parse decodes → in v1.1.0 bullet 4, which the September file kept as an entity. The September entries are carried over unchanged. Three releases are new: v1.3.0 (2 Oct), v1.3.1 and v1.3.1.1 (4 Oct).

internal_releases_before_1_0.note: Pre-1.0 releases were never shipped to anyone outside; the public log restarts at 1.0 on 27 August 2026 rather than continuing from v2.365.0.

releases.title: Told when the month’s runs are used up
bullet_leads: When your free runs for the month are used up, Atlas now emails you once.
Runs skipped for the monthly limit no longer show up later as missed runs.
A search typed as a question finds an answer.

releases.title: From first try to first email
bullet_leads: On a phone, the box that runs a task on the home page now sits right under the headline.
When a try on the home page fails, you can still keep the sentence.
A new page, try-atlas.app/stocks, is for anyone who checks the market close by hand.
Links that open the app with a sentence to try no longer cover the answer with the welcome tour.
The sign-up panel shows the sentence you are signing up to keep.
A task brought over from the home page or the stocks page can send its first email straight away.
The sentence you brought over from a try stays in the app until the task is saved.
A task’s first email says what it is and when the next one comes.
Stopping Atlas’s emails takes one click, with no sign-in.
Price tasks come back with live prices even when many run at once.
Free tries are counted per visitor.
A run you start yourself that fails no longer uses one of your runs.
The site’s promises now match what Atlas does.

releases.title: Try it, then keep it
bullet_leads: The home page runs a task before you sign up, and the sentence is already typed for you.
“Email me this every weekday” turns that try into a task of your own.
The schedule Atlas spotted while you were trying it out is the schedule you get after signing up.
“Try a sample task” sets up a morning task that says when it runs.
Coming back to the app, you see what ran while you were away.
Links in Atlas’s emails open the task they are about, even when you have to sign in first.
A failed run offers Run again right under the error, and Open Settings when the error is about your API key.
Deleting is harder to do by accident, and it never fails silently.
The keyboard goes where you expect.
More of the app fits a phone, and a few rough edges are gone.
A task asking why several stocks moved keeps headlines for every one of them.
Atlas now counts how visitors get from the home page to their first task, using one first-party cookie.

releases.title: Real prices, real headlines
bullet_leads: “Apple stock price” comes back with Apple’s actual quote and how far it has moved today.
“Why did Nvidia drop today” is answered with the day’s headlines under the price.
“Bitcoin and Solana price” reads live figures too, and asking again a minute later costs no second look-up.
A price task that lands in a busy minute waits its turn instead of failing.
Signed-out visitors get the app’s solid top bar, the scroll-to-top button and every keyboard shortcut, and Escape closes the shortcuts panel again.
Links inside a Settings card are painted in the app’s own accent colour instead of the browser’s default blue.
A history entry’s preview reads as plain sentences instead of raw markdown, and Show full opens the whole result on a desktop screen as well as on a phone.
A task Atlas paused after three failed runs in a row now tells you how to start it again.
A scheduled run that can only send you the raw text it fetched cleans that text first.

releases.title: The app fits a phone
bullet_leads: A message from Atlas no longer covers the New Task button on a phone.
The app’s top bar stays readable in dark mode once you scroll.
The buttons you press to get started are on screen on the smallest phones, with no scrolling.
Nothing in the app is set smaller than 12 pixels on a phone, and the controls are big enough to hit.
Task names and instructions show more of themselves in the list on a phone.
The latest result is already open when you look at a task on a phone.
The list of tasks that slides in on a phone has its New Task button back, and pressing it puts you straight into the box.
The upgrade window fits a phone, and the way out of it stays in reach.

releases.title: Settings that fit, and controls that answer
bullet_leads: The Settings sidebar shows all of its tabs at once, instead of hiding the last few below the fold.
Settings has a What’s new card, so the latest releases are readable without leaving Atlas.
Deleting a saved API key now sticks.
The invite-friends card no longer shows in Settings on a Pro plan.
The AI Usage card appears only when you are running on an API key of your own.
A control you press now shows that it was pressed, instead of looking dead until the server answers.
The logo inside the app is the same brand mark as the one on the Atlas home page.
A task that asks for news comes back with a round-up, not a single story.

releases.title: Approximate location
bullet_leads: A task that asks about where you are is answered for your city, and the answer names it.
Settings has a Location card — detected from your connection, set by you, or off.
What Atlas keeps is a city, and the privacy page and the FAQ say so.
The try-it box on the home page answers a placeless ask for the city your connection suggests.
A step inside a workflow task that invents a figure under a source it never opened is marked unsourced.

releases.title: The chart, the export and the briefing agree
bullet_leads: The Analytics tab, its CSV export and the run briefing now score the same runs.
A workflow task whose steps measure different things now shows each step’s own chart.
A task’s chart reads the figure that is about its own subject.
Settings scrolls smoothly again.
The template gallery no longer freezes on Show all.
A figure invented under a source Atlas never opened is marked unsourced.
A task that asks about where you are, without naming a place, asks which city.
Tasks about a market, a pricing page or the week’s developments are looked up rather than remembered.

releases.title: Analytics that chart the right number
bullet_leads: A task’s chart now tracks one measurement, and it is the one the task is about.
The Analytics tab charts the figure a result leads with.
A fall written with a typographic minus sign is charted as a fall.
A task that returns prose says there is nothing to record.
A failed run contributes no number — not to the CSV export, not to the figures behind the briefing.
The trend word agrees with the change beside it.
A long history draws its chart without holding up the rest of the app.
Run emails read the way the answer was written.
A run email’s subject line fits in an inbox.
The daily and weekly digests read like the emails around them.
A digest item’s one-line excerpt stops ending on a list of sources.
Every Atlas email’s preview line fits the width a phone shows.
A run email stops printing the answer twice.
A result full of blank lines no longer holds up its own email.
A push about a finished run opens the task it is about.
A push about a run that produced no answer says so, instead of showing one.
A length you ask for is a limit, not a suggestion.
An answer never opens by explaining what the model cannot reach.
A length you ask for “each” of caps each item, not the whole answer.
The demo stops printing a title over the answer.
Atlas looks things up when you ask about the weather, and stops looking when there is nothing to look up.
A run after a refusal starts clean.
An answer that declines to answer is marked as one.
A refusal that names the date you asked about is still marked as a refusal.
A flagged answer says how many times the model was asked, instead of promising a retry that never happened.
A preview answers the way the scheduled run will.
Replying to a digest with nothing new leaves your task alone.
A reply to a run email is read however you typed it.
More of a reply gets read, and it is read in any language.
Crypto prices stop failing in bursts.
Failed runs that still cost tokens are counted and priced.
The demo counts a failed run the same way whichever way it failed.
A workflow step that ends on a yes/no verdict is no longer marked as cut off.
The one-line briefing on a run stops citing sources the answer never named.
A briefing compares like with like, and names the number it compares against.
A run that comes back with nothing is briefed as such.
The briefing after a failed run says what failed.
A briefing is written at the quality tier your plan sets.
A briefing is never longer than the answer it introduces.
An alert now needs six readings of the same measure behind it.
The anomaly email is judged on the same readings as the rest of the task.
The briefing on a run compares against readings that held a real number.
A run that produced no answer is not scored against the task’s history.
Ask the help assistant about a feature by name and it finds the page about that feature.
An answer buried deep in a long page is found there rather than refused.
The help assistant answers a deliberately shaped question in the same time as an ordinary one.
Quieter fixes underneath.

releases.title: GitHub tasks (beta)
bullet_leads: Tasks can read your GitHub, in beta — tell us when one misreads a repo.
Read access only, and the token stays yours.
No token, no guessing.

releases.title: Better answers
bullet_leads: Every result now opens with the answer.
A recurring run now knows what its last one said.
When Atlas can fetch the real data, it fetches it first.
A price fetched outside trading hours says so.
“Today” means today where you are.
When a run goes wrong, the result says so — and says what Atlas did about it.
Those notes are more accurate than they were.
Workflows: every step is graded, and the last one leads with the bottom line.
What a briefing remembers is checked before it is kept.
One model having a bad day is no longer your problem.
A run that fails says what failed, in Atlas’s words.
Schedules and limits hold up better under load.
Importing tasks tells you what it did not import.
An address that keeps bouncing is retired.
You can see where a link in an email goes.
Webhook deliveries are signed.
Analytics reads a period now, not a number of runs.
A dollar chart is plotted as change, and big totals are written short.
A chart plots the figure, not the clock.
Fewer false alarms, without missing the real ones.
Preview runs the prompt that will actually run.
A result cites only what it actually retrieved.
A “Sources” list the model wrote for itself is stripped whichever model you brought.
A fake source planted inside a fetched page is not cited as one.
You can see what your account is spending.
Nothing is kept forever.
Teams.
The app on a phone.
When the app cannot load, it says so.
The docs say what actually happens.
Under the hood.

releases.title: Invites
bullet_leads: Share Atlas and both sides get more runs.
How it works.
Bonus runs are a monthly allowance, not a permanent upgrade.
Settings → Invites now reads “3 of 10 friends credited this month”.
And it now says what reaching ten means.
The docs and the FAQ say the same thing.
Your run limit is worked out per account now, instead of being a fixed number.
Invites are for new accounts.
Fixed: the Run now button in result emails used the wrong limit.
Also in this release.

releases.title: Atlas 1.0
bullet_leads: Atlas is open. You describe a job in plain words, tell it when to run, and it runs on its own and sends you the result.
What is built.
One note on the number.
